title: To Beat Cigarette Addiction, More Health Experts Are Embracing Vapes
excerpt: Growing clinical evidence shows e-cigarettes help smokers quit at higher rates than traditional therapies, forcing a rethink of public health strategy even as youth vaping concerns persist.
body:
• A major Australian clinical trial found 28% of smokers using vapes quit after six months, compared to under 10% using nicotine gum or lozenges
  • A UK study showed dual users of cigarettes and vapes were 4.5 times more likely to eventually quit smoking entirely
  • The US National Institute on Drug Abuse and a 2024 Cochrane review now acknowledge e-cigarettes outperform traditional nicotine replacement therapy
  • Regulators face a balancing act: flavoured vape bans may reduce youth uptake but push adult smokers back to deadlier cigarettes

A growing body of clinical evidence is pushing public health authorities toward a position once considered heretical: that e-cigarettes, long demonised for fuelling a youth nicotine epidemic, may be the most effective tool available for helping adult smokers quit.

The shift is being driven by a string of randomised controlled trials and systematic reviews that consistently show vaping outperforms the nicotine patches, gums and lozenges that have been the standard of care for decades. It is a debate with direct relevance to India, where an estimated 267 million tobacco users face some of the world's highest rates of oral and lung cancers, and where e-cigarettes were banned outright in 2019.

The Clinical Case Strengthens

The most significant recent evidence comes from a trial published in the Annals of Internal Medicine in July 2025. Researchers at the University of New South Wales recruited more than 1,000 Australians receiving government assistance and randomly assigned them to flavoured nicotine vapes or traditional nicotine replacement therapy (NRT).

The results were striking. After six months, 28.4% of the vaping group remained smoke-free, compared to just 9.6% of those given gum or lozenges. The effect held regardless of age, gender, nicotine dependence level, or mental health history.

"Vapes, in addition to delivering nicotine, provide some of the sensory and behavioural aspects that people miss when they quit smoking."

— Ryan Courtney, Associate Professor, University of New South Wales

A separate UK study published in Nicotine & Tobacco Research in December 2025 analysed 886 adult smokers and found that those who continued using both cigarettes and vapes were nearly 4.5 times as likely to stop smoking entirely within a month, and equally likely to halve their cigarette consumption within a year.

Institutional Attitudes Are Shifting

These findings have begun to reshape official positions. In September 2025, the US National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) published a detailed assessment acknowledging that vaping "does not present the worst health risks associated with combustible tobacco" and that randomised trials show e-cigarettes are "successful as smoking cessation aids, specifically when they are provided free as a therapeutic intervention."

A 2024 Cochrane systematic review, widely regarded as the gold standard for medical evidence, concluded that nicotine e-cigarettes help people stop smoking for at least six months and outperform NRT. The UK's National Health Service already recommends e-cigarettes as a quit aid, while the American Society of Addiction Medicine recognises switching from cigarettes to vapes as a harm reduction approach.

The Youth Vaping Dilemma

The enthusiasm is far from universal. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention maintains that "dual use is not an effective way to safeguard health," and youth uptake remains a central concern. About 8% of US high school students reported e-cigarette use in 2024, down from 10% the previous year.

A Harvard panel in September 2025 highlighted the core tension. Joseph Daval, a researcher at Harvard's Program on Regulation, Therapeutics, and Law, noted that while bans on flavoured vapes may decrease youth use, "these gains may come at the expense of increased use among adults of combustible tobacco products, which remains the leading cause of preventable death in the US."

"There's myriad research pointing to e-cigarettes as an effective smoking cessation aid."

— Abigail Friedman, Associate Professor of Public Health, Yale University

Why It Matters for the Diaspora

India banned the sale, manufacture, import and advertising of e-cigarettes under the Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Act in 2019, citing youth protection concerns. The ban means Indian smokers, who number in the hundreds of millions and face devastating cancer rates from both cigarettes and smokeless tobacco, are cut off from a cessation tool that multiple Western health bodies now endorse.

For diaspora Indians, the debate is also personal. Many live in countries where vaping is legal and regulated, while family members back home remain dependent on combustible tobacco with no access to emerging alternatives. The growing evidence base adds urgency to calls for India to revisit its blanket prohibition in favour of a regulated framework that restricts youth access while allowing adult smokers a pathway off cigarettes.

What Comes Next

Researchers caution that long-term safety data on vaping remain limited, and the Australian trial noted that 58% of successful quitters continued vaping at the end of the study period, raising questions about whether e-cigarettes simply replace one nicotine dependency with another. But with combustible tobacco killing more than 8 million people globally each year according to the WHO, the clinical consensus is tilting toward pragmatism over perfection.
nri_angle: India's 2019 blanket ban on e-cigarettes leaves hundreds of millions of smokers without access to a cessation tool now endorsed by multiple Western health bodies, a policy gap felt acutely by diaspora families.
